claim: In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and animal models of ALS, including SOD1-G93A mice, disassembly of the neuromuscular synapse precedes motor neuron loss.
source: In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and animal models of ALS, including SOD1-G93A mice, disassembly of the neuromuscular synapse precedes motor neuron loss and is sufficient to cause a decline in motor function that culminates in lethal respiratory paralysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Fischer et al., 2004; Schaefer et al., 2005; Pun et al., 2006) and established knowledge about ALS pathology.

claim: Disassembly of the neuromuscular synapse is sufficient to cause a decline in motor function that culminates in lethal respiratory paralysis in SOD1-G93A mice.
source: In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and animal models of ALS, including SOD1-G93A mice, disassembly of the neuromuscular synapse precedes motor neuron loss and is sufficient to cause a decline in motor function that culminates in lethal respiratory paralysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and established knowledge about ALS pathology.

claim: The agonist antibody to MuSK, delivered after disease onset, slowed muscle denervation in SOD1-G93A mice.
source: The agonist antibody, delivered after disease onset, slowed muscle denervation, promoting motor neuron survival, improving motor system output, and extending the lifespan of SOD1-G93A mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 4 showing reduced denervation in antibody-treated mice.

claim: The agonist antibody to MuSK promoted motor neuron survival in SOD1-G93A mice.
source: The agonist antibody, delivered after disease onset, slowed muscle denervation, promoting motor neuron survival, improving motor system output, and extending the lifespan of SOD1-G93A mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6B showing increased motor neuron counts in antibody-treated mice.

claim: The agonist antibody to MuSK improved motor system output in SOD1-G93A mice.
source: The agonist antibody, delivered after disease onset, slowed muscle denervation, promoting motor neuron survival, improving motor system output, and extending the lifespan of SOD1-G93A mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5 showing improved CMAP responses in antibody-treated mice.

claim: The agonist antibody to MuSK extended the lifespan of SOD1-G93A mice.
source: The agonist antibody, delivered after disease onset, slowed muscle denervation, promoting motor neuron survival, improving motor system output, and extending the lifespan of SOD1-G93A mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6C,D showing increased survival in antibody-treated mice.

claim: The loss of neuromuscular synapses occurs prior to the loss of motor neurons in both familial and sporadic forms of ALS.
source: Although motor neuron cell death is a hallmark feature of ALS, the loss of neuromuscular synapses occurs prior to the loss of motor neurons and is the primary cause of motor paralysis in both familial and sporadic forms of ALS (Fischer et al., 2004; Schaefer et al., 2005; Pun et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: The loss of neuromuscular synapses is the primary cause of motor paralysis in both familial and sporadic forms of ALS.
source: Although motor neuron cell death is a hallmark feature of ALS, the loss of neuromuscular synapses occurs prior to the loss of motor neurons and is the primary cause of motor paralysis in both familial and sporadic forms of ALS (Fischer et al., 2004; Schaefer et al., 2005; Pun et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Transgenic mice bearing dominant mutations in the human SOD1 gene, including SOD1-G93A mice, recapitulate the hallmark features of ALS.
source: Transgenic mice bearing dominant mutations in the human SOD1 gene, including SOD1-G93A mice, recapitulate the hallmark features of ALS and provide the most thoroughly studied animal model for ALS (Vinsant et al., 2013a; Vinsant et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: SOD1-G93A mice provide the most thoroughly studied animal model for ALS.
source: Transgenic mice bearing dominant mutations in the human SOD1 gene, including SOD1-G93A mice, recapitulate the hallmark features of ALS and provide the most thoroughly studied animal model for ALS (Vinsant et al., 2013a; Vinsant et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Detachment of motor nerve terminals is the primary cause for paralysis in SOD1-G93A mice.
source: Moreover, because detachment of motor nerve terminals is the primary cause for paralysis in SOD1-G93A mice, SOD1-G93A mice represent a clinically relevant model for ALS.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about the SOD1-G93A mouse model.

claim: SOD1-G93A mice represent a clinically relevant model for ALS.
source: Moreover, because detachment of motor nerve terminals is the primary cause for paralysis in SOD1-G93A mice, SOD1-G93A mice represent a clinically relevant model for ALS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity between the pathology in SOD1-G93A mice and human ALS.

claim: Lrp4 is the muscle receptor for the critical neuronal ligand, Agrin.
source: Lrp4, a member of the LDL receptor family, is the muscle receptor for the critical neuronal ligand, Agrin (Kim et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Clustered Lrp4 signals back to motor axons to stimulate their attachment and differentiation.
source: Clustered Lrp4 then signals back to motor axons to stimulate their attachment and differentiation (Yumoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Recessive mutations in Agrin, Lrp4 or Musk cause congenital myasthenia.
source: Recessive mutations in Agrin, Lrp4 or Musk cause congenital myasthenia, a group of neuromuscular disorders, distinct from ALS, which compromise the structure and function of neuromuscular synapses and lead to muscle weakness and fatigue (Engel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Autoantibodies to Agrin, Lrp4, or MuSK cause myasthenia gravis (MG).
source: Moreover, autoantibodies to Agrin, Lrp4, or MuSK cause myasthenia gravis (MG), which is likewise distinct from ALS (Gilhus and Verschuuren, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In MuSK MG, the pathogenic antibodies are usually directed to the first Ig-like domain in MuSK and reduce MuSK phosphorylation by impairing binding between Lrp4 and MuSK.
source: In MuSK MG, the pathogenic antibodies are usually directed to the first Ig-like domain in MuSK and reduce MuSK phosphorylation by impairing binding between Lrp4 and MuSK (Huijbers et al., 2013; Koneczny et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Defects in the MuSK signaling pathway are not associated with ALS.
source: Although defects in the MuSK signaling pathway are not associated with ALS, increasing MuSK gene expression stabilizes neuromuscular synapses in SOD1-G93A mice, reducing the extent of muscle denervation and improving motor function (Pérez-García and Burden, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about ALS pathology.

claim: Increasing MuSK gene expression stabilizes neuromuscular synapses in SOD1-G93A mice, reducing the extent of muscle denervation and improving motor function.
source: Although defects in the MuSK signaling pathway are not associated with ALS, increasing MuSK gene expression stabilizes neuromuscular synapses in SOD1-G93A mice, reducing the extent of muscle denervation and improving motor function (Pérez-García and Burden, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Antibodies #13 and #22, re-engineered as human IgG1 molecules, stimulated MuSK tyrosine phosphorylation in the C2 mouse muscle cell line.
source: We confirmed that antibodies #13 and #22, re-engineered as human IgG1 molecules, stimulated MuSK tyrosine phosphorylation in the C2 mouse muscle cell line (Figure 1A), whereas antibody #21, as well as a control IgG1 antibody to ragweed pollen, failed to stimulate MuSK phosphorylation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Antibody #21 and a control IgG1 antibody to ragweed pollen failed to stimulate MuSK phosphorylation in the C2 mouse muscle cell line.
source: We confirmed that antibodies #13 and #22, re-engineered as human IgG1 molecules, stimulated MuSK tyrosine phosphorylation in the C2 mouse muscle cell line (Figure 1A), whereas antibody #21, as well as a control IgG1 antibody to ragweed pollen, failed to stimulate MuSK phosphorylation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Full-length ecto-MuSK and the MuSK Fz-like domain alone bind MuSK antibody #13 in a dose-dependent and saturable manner.
source: The scatter plot shows that full-length ecto-MuSK (), as well as the MuSK Fz-like domain alone () bind MuSK antibody #13 in a dose-dependent and saturable manner; in contrast, the first three Ig-like domains in MuSK () fail to bind the MuSK agonist antibody (n = 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The first three Ig-like domains in MuSK fail to bind the MuSK agonist antibody #13.
source: The scatter plot shows that full-length ecto-MuSK (), as well as the MuSK Fz-like domain alone () bind MuSK antibody #13 in a dose-dependent and saturable manner; in contrast, the first three Ig-like domains in MuSK () fail to bind the MuSK agonist antibody (n = 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Agrin stimulates MuSK phosphorylation in wild type but not Lrp4 mutant myotubes.
source: Agrin stimulates MuSK phosphorylation in wild type but not Lrp4 mutant myotubes, whereas MuSK agonist antibody #13 stimulates MuSK phosphorylation in both wild type and Lrp4 mutant myotubes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: MuSK agonist antibody #13 stimulates MuSK phosphorylation in both wild type and Lrp4 mutant myotubes.
source: Agrin stimulates MuSK phosphorylation in wild type but not Lrp4 mutant myotubes, whereas MuSK agonist antibody #13 stimulates MuSK phosphorylation in both wild type and Lrp4 mutant myotubes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The agonist antibody binds the Fz-like domain in MuSK, force-dimerizing and stimulating MuSK phosphorylation, independent of Lrp4.
source: In contrast to the Agrin-dependent mechanism for activating MuSK, the agonist antibody binds the Fz-like domain in MuSK, force-dimerizing and stimulating MuSK phosphorylation, independent of Lrp4 (Figure 1B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B, 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Fz-like domain is dispensable for synapse formation in mice.
source: Importantly, the Fz-like domain is dispensable for synapse formation in mice (Remédio et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Neuromuscular synapses were labeled specifically by the MuSK agonist antibody.
source: Figure 2A shows that neuromuscular synapses were labeled specifically by the MuSK agonist antibody.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MuSK staining was evident as early as 3 days after a single injection of the agonist antibody.
source: MuSK staining was evident as early as 3 days (Figure 2Aiv-vi), and staining persisted for at least 7 days after the single injection (Figure 2A,vii-ix).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MuSK staining persisted for at least 7 days after a single injection of the agonist antibody.
source: MuSK staining was evident as early as 3 days (Figure 2Aiv-vi), and staining persisted for at least 7 days after the single injection (Figure 2A,vii-ix).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The organization of AChRs and nerve terminals appeared normal after MuSK agonist antibody injection.
source: The organization of AChRs and nerve terminals appeared normal (Figure 2A,ii,v,viii), indicating that the MuSK agonist antibody did not disturb major features of synaptic differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The MuSK agonist antibody did not disturb major features of synaptic differentiation.
source: The organization of AChRs and nerve terminals appeared normal (Figure 2A,ii,v,viii), indicating that the MuSK agonist antibody did not disturb major features of synaptic differentiation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that AChR and nerve terminal organization appeared normal.

claim: Visual observation of the antibody-injected mice did not reveal overt behavioral abnormalities.
source: Moreover, visual observation of the antibody-injected mice did not reveal overt behavioral abnormalities, indicating that the MuSK agonist antibody was well tolerated by the mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data from the study.

claim: The MuSK agonist antibody was well tolerated by the mice.
source: Moreover, visual observation of the antibody-injected mice did not reveal overt behavioral abnormalities, indicating that the MuSK agonist antibody was well tolerated by the mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that no overt behavioral abnormalities were detected.

claim: 2 mg/kg of the agonist antibody was sufficient to saturate MuSK labeling at the synapse.
source: Two mg/kg of the agonist antibody was sufficient to saturate MuSK labeling at the synapse (Figure 2B) and increase MuSK tyrosine phosphorylation in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 2 mg/kg of the agonist antibody increased MuSK tyrosine phosphorylation in vivo.
source: Two mg/kg of the agonist antibody was sufficient to saturate MuSK labeling at the synapse (Figure 2B) and increase MuSK tyrosine phosphorylation in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The half-life of the injected antibody in blood was approximately 12 days.
source: We measured the pharmacokinetic properties of the injected antibody and found that the half-life of the injected antibody in blood was ~12 days (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The antibody exhibited linear clearance for 21 days after antibody injection.
source: The antibody exhibited linear clearance for 21 days after antibody injection, indicating that exposure could be maintained over several weeks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The mouse immune system did not recognize and clear the antibody, which contained a human Fc region, from the circulation over a three-week time period.
source: In addition, these results demonstrated that the mouse immune system did not recognize and clear the antibody, which contained a human Fc region, from the circulation over this three-week time period (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of linear clearance over 21 days.

claim: In SOD1-G93A mice, denervation of limb muscles begins at P50.
source: In SOD1-G93A mice, denervation of limb muscles begins at P50, whereas denervation of the diaphragm muscle begins a month later (Pun et al., 2006; Rocha et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: In SOD1-G93A mice, denervation of the diaphragm muscle begins at approximately P80.
source: In SOD1-G93A mice, denervation of limb muscles begins at P50, whereas denervation of the diaphragm muscle begins a month later (Pun et al., 2006; Rocha et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the statement that diaphragm denervation begins a month after P50.

claim: Denervation of the diaphragm muscle is responsible for lethal respiratory paralysis in SOD1-G93A mice.
source: Because denervation of the diaphragm muscle is responsible for lethal respiratory paralysis, we focused our analysis on innervation of this muscle.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about the role of the diaphragm in respiration.

claim: Denervation was evident in SOD1-G93A mice as early as P90.
source: Denervation was evident in SOD1-G93A mice as early as P90 (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: From P90 to P110, the extent of full innervation decreased from 77.3% to 18.1% in female SOD1-G93A mice.
source: From P90 to P110, the extent of full innervation, defined as perfect apposition of nerve terminals and the AChR-rich postsynaptic membrane, decreased from 77.3% to 18.1% in female and from 53.1% to 16.1% in male SOD1-G93A mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: From P90 to P110, the extent of full innervation decreased from 53.1% to 16.1% in male SOD1-G93A mice.
source: From P90 to P110, the extent of full innervation, defined as perfect apposition of nerve terminals and the AChR-rich postsynaptic membrane, decreased from 77.3% to 18.1% in female and from 53.1% to 16.1% in male SOD1-G93A mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: From P90 to P110, the extent of complete denervation increased from 2.3% to 41% in female SOD1-G93A mice.
source: Likewise, the extent of complete denervation increased from 2.3% to 41% in female and from 16.7% to 24.4% in male SOD1-G93A mice over this twenty-day period (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: From P90 to P110, the extent of complete denervation increased from 16.7% to 24.4% in male SOD1-G93A mice.
source: Likewise, the extent of complete denervation increased from 2.3% to 41% in female and from 16.7% to 24.4% in male SOD1-G93A mice over this twenty-day period (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A single dose of the MuSK agonist antibody increased the number of fully innervated synapses by 2.7-fold in female SOD1-G93A mice.
source: We found that a single dose of the MuSK agonist antibody increased the number of fully innervated synapses by 2.7- and 2.5-fold in female and male SOD1-G93A mice, respectively, and decreased the number of fully denervated synapses by 3.7- and 2.3-fold in female and male SOD1-G93A mice, respectively (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: A single dose of the MuSK agonist antibody increased the number of fully innervated synapses by 2.5-fold in male SOD1-G93A mice.
source: We found that a single dose of the MuSK agonist antibody increased the number of fully innervated synapses by 2.7- and 2.5-fold in female and male SOD1-G93A mice, respectively, and decreased the number of fully denervated synapses by 3.7- and 2.3-fold in female and male SOD1-G93A mice, respectively (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: A single dose of the MuSK agonist antibody decreased the number of fully denervated synapses by 3.7-fold in female SOD1-G93A mice.
source: We found that a single dose of the MuSK agonist antibody increased the number of fully innervated synapses by 2.7- and 2.5-fold in female and male SOD1-G93A mice, respectively, and decreased the number of fully denervated synapses by 3.7- and 2.3-fold in female and male SOD1-G93A mice, respectively (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: A single dose of the MuSK agonist antibody decreased the number of fully denervated synapses by 2.3-fold in male SOD1-G93A mice.
source: We found that a single dose of the MuSK agonist antibody increased the number of fully innervated synapses by 2.7- and 2.5-fold in female and male SOD1-G93A mice, respectively, and decreased the number of fully denervated synapses by 3.7- and 2.3-fold in female and male SOD1-G93A mice, respectively (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: The MuSK agonist antibody, introduced after disease onset, decreased motor axon withdrawal from the diaphragm muscle.
source: These findings demonstrated that the MuSK agonist antibody, introduced after disease onset, decreased motor axon withdrawal from the diaphragm muscle.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing reduced denervation in antibody-treated mice.

claim: The reverse chimera MuSK agonist antibody halted progressive loss of fully innervated synapses from P114 to P162 in SOD1-G93A mice.
source: This progressive loss was halted by injection of the MuSK agonist antibody, as the number of fully innervated synapses was largely unchanged (40–50%) from P114 to P162 in SOD1-G93A mice injected with the MuSK agonist antibody (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The reverse chimera MuSK agonist antibody prevented the progressive increase in fully denervated synapses from P114 to P162 in SOD1-G93A mice.
source: Similarly, the number of fully denervated synapses continued to increase from P114 through P162 in SOD1-G93A mice injected with the control antibody, whereas this progressive increase was prevented by the MuSK agonist antibody (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The MuSK agonist antibody prevented further synaptic loss and preserved synapses for at least 50 days after signs of denervation and disease were evident in SOD1-G93A mice.
source: These findings indicate that the MuSK agonist antibody prevented further synaptic loss and preserved synapses for at least 50 days after signs of denervation and disease were evident in SOD1-G93A mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing stable innervation levels from P114 to P162.

claim: The extent of nerve terminal coverage was 34% greater at partially innervated synapses in mice injected with the MuSK agonist antibody compared to control antibody.
source: Although the number of partially innervated synapses was similar in SOD1-G93A mice injected with the control or MuSK agonist antibody (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), the extent of nerve terminal coverage was 34% greater at partially innervated synapses in mice injected with the MuSK agonist antibody (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The MuSK agonist antibody increased both full innervation as well as nerve terminal coverage at partially innervated synapses in SOD1-G93A mice.
source: Thus, the MuSK agonist antibody increased both full innervation as well as nerve terminal coverage at partially innervated synapses in SOD1-G93A mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing increased full innervation and increased nerve terminal coverage at partially innervated synapses.

claim: There was no significant difference in the amplitude of the first CMAP between SOD1-G93A mice injected with the MuSK agonist antibody or the control antibody to GP120.
source: We found no significant difference in the amplitude of the first CMAP between SOD1-G93A mice injected with the MuSK agonist antibody or the control antibody to GP120 (anti-GP120-treated males: 5.95 ± 1.14 mV; anti-MuSK-treated males: 5.93 ± 0.52 mV; anti-GP120-treated females: 4.95 ± 0.54 mV; anti-MuSK-treated females: 5.81 ± 0.63 mV).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CMAP measurements.

claim: Repetitive stimulation of the phrenic nerve at 20 Hz led to a rapid and severe decline in the amplitude of the CMAP in SOD1-G93A mice chronically injected with the control antibody to GP120.
source: We found a rapid and severe decline in the amplitude of the CMAP, indicative of synaptic dysfunction and denervation, in SOD1-G93A mice chronically injected with the control antibody to GP120.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The decline in CMAP amplitude during 20 Hz stimulation was far less severe in SOD1-G93A mice treated with the MuSK agonist antibody compared to control antibody.
source: In contrast, the decline in CMAP amplitude was far less severe in SOD1-G93A mice treated with the MuSK agonist antibody, demonstrating that the MuSK agonist antibody improved neuromuscular function (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The MuSK agonist antibody improved neuromuscular function in SOD1-G93A mice.
source: In contrast, the decline in CMAP amplitude was far less severe in SOD1-G93A mice treated with the MuSK agonist antibody, demonstrating that the MuSK agonist antibody improved neuromuscular function (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of improved CMAP responses in antibody-treated mice.

claim: After 5 seconds of 20 Hz stimulation, the MuSK agonist improved CMAP amplitude by 13.6% in females and by 31.7% in males.
source: After 5 s, the MuSK agonist improved CMAP amplitude by 13.6% in females and by 31.7% in males (n = 6–7; p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: 50 Hz stimulation of the phrenic nerve in SOD1-G93A mice injected with the control antibody to GP120 led to frequent failures to elicit a CMAP.
source: Moreover, repetitive stimulation of the phrenic nerve at a more challenging frequency (50 Hz) led to frequent failures to elicit a CMAP in SOD1-G93A mice injected with the control antibody to GP120.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: CMAP failures during 50 Hz stimulation were less frequent in SOD1-G93A mice injected with the MuSK agonist antibody, similar to wild type mice.
source: Such failures were less frequent in SOD1-G93A mice injected with the MuSK agonist antibody, similar to wild type mice (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The MuSK agonist antibody reduced the number of CMAP failures by 88% in females and 70% in males during 1 min of 50 Hz stimulation.
source: The MuSK agonist antibody reduced the number of failures by 88% in females and 70% in males during 1 min of stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The maintenance of neuromuscular synapses, stimulated by the MuSK agonist antibody, led to improved reliability of synaptic transmission and output of the diaphragm muscle in SOD1-G93A mice.
source: In either case, the maintenance of neuromuscular synapses, stimulated by the MuSK agonist antibody, led to improved reliability of synaptic transmission and output of the critically important diaphragm muscle in SOD1-G93A mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing improved CMAP responses and reduced failures in antibody-treated mice.

claim: The MuSK agonist antibody increased the number of motor neurons by 31% to 57% at P138 in SOD1-G93A mice.
source: The MuSK agonist antibody increased the number of motor neurons by 31% to 57% at P138 (Figure 6B), during the peak period of motor neuron cell death in SOD1-G93A mice when approximately half of spinal motor neurons have been lost (Vinsant et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: P138 is during the peak period of motor neuron cell death in SOD1-G93A mice when approximately half of spinal motor neurons have been lost.
source: The MuSK agonist antibody increased the number of motor neurons by 31% to 57% at P138 (Figure 6B), during the peak period of motor neuron cell death in SOD1-G93A mice when approximately half of spinal motor neurons have been lost (Vinsant et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Increasing retrograde signaling after disease onset preserves neuromuscular synapses and promotes survival of spinal motor neurons in SOD1-G93A mice.
source: These findings demonstrate that increasing retrograde signaling after disease onset not only preserves neuromuscular synapses but also promotes survival of spinal motor neurons in SOD1-G93A mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing both preserved synapses and increased motor neuron survival in antibody-treated mice.

claim: Female SOD1-G93A mice injected with the control antibody to GP120 had an average lifespan of 169 days.
source: Female SOD1-G93A mice injected with the control antibody to GP120 had an average lifespan of 169 days (see Materials and methods), whereas male SOD1-G93A mice injected with the control antibody had an average lifespan of 157.5 days (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Male SOD1-G93A mice injected with the control antibody to GP120 had an average lifespan of 157.5 days.
source: Female SOD1-G93A mice injected with the control antibody to GP120 had an average lifespan of 169 days (see Materials and methods), whereas male SOD1-G93A mice injected with the control antibody had an average lifespan of 157.5 days (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Chronic injection with the MuSK agonist antibody prolonged survival of female SOD1-G93A mice by 7 days.
source: Chronic injection with the MuSK agonist antibody prolonged survival of female and male SOD1-G93A mice by 7 (p<0.05) and 10 days (p<0.001), respectively (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Chronic injection with the MuSK agonist antibody prolonged survival of male SOD1-G93A mice by 10 days.
source: Chronic injection with the MuSK agonist antibody prolonged survival of female and male SOD1-G93A mice by 7 (p<0.05) and 10 days (p<0.001), respectively (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: The MuSK agonist antibody, introduced after disease onset, slowed the disassembly of neuromuscular synapses, improved motor output of the diaphragm muscle and extended the lifespan of SOD1-G93A mice.
source: Thus, the MuSK agonist antibody, introduced after disease onset, slowed the disassembly of neuromuscular synapses, improved motor output of the diaphragm muscle and extended the lifespan of SOD1-G93A mice.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: An agonist antibody to MuSK decreases muscle denervation, improves motor system output, reduces motor neuron loss and extends survival in an aggressive mouse model of ALS.
source: Here, we describe a therapeutic approach designed to slow the loss of motor innervation to muscle by targeting a well-defined molecule and mechanism for forming and maintaining neuromuscular synapses. We show that an agonist antibody to MuSK, introduced after disease onset, decreases muscle denervation, improves motor system output, reduces motor neuron loss and extends survival in an aggressive mouse model of ALS.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Anti-sense RNA directed toward SOD1 is currently being tested as a promising therapeutic for ALS caused by mutations in SOD1.
source: Anti-sense RNA directed toward SOD1 is currently being tested as a promising therapeutic for ALS caused by mutations in SOD1 (Miller et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: More than 80% of ALS patients are diagnosed with sporadic ALS.
source: However, >80% of ALS patients are diagnosed with sporadic ALS, so strategies to inactivate a single culprit gene are not tenable for most cases of ALS.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about ALS epidemiology.

claim: Synaptic loss and muscle denervation are common to sporadic as well as familial forms of ALS.
source: Because synaptic loss and muscle denervation are common to sporadic as well as familial forms of ALS, the approach described here has the potential to be effective for both forms of ALS.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about ALS pathology.

claim: Adenoviral expression of Dok-7 extends longevity of SOD1-G93A mice.
source: Consistent with this idea, adenoviral expression of Dok-7, an inside-outside activator of MuSK, not only extends longevity of SOD1-G93A mice but also provides benefit in other mouse models of neuromuscular disease, including congenital myasthenia and Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (Miyoshi et al., 2017; Arimura et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Adenoviral expression of Dok-7 provides benefit in mouse models of congenital myasthenia and Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy.
source: Consistent with this idea, adenoviral expression of Dok-7, an inside-outside activator of MuSK, not only extends longevity of SOD1-G93A mice but also provides benefit in other mouse models of neuromuscular disease, including congenital myasthenia and Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (Miyoshi et al., 2017; Arimura et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Synaptic loss occurs early during disease progression in Alzheimer's disease, Huntington's disease, Parkinson's disease, Frontotemporal dementia and Spinal Muscular Atrophy.
source: Further, there is increasing evidence that synaptic loss occurs early during disease progression in other neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease, Huntington's disease, Parkinson's disease and Frontotemporal dementia and Spinal Muscular Atrophy (Henstridge et al., 2016), so similar strategies, designed to preserve synapses, may slow progression in these diseases as well.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Denervation is the cause of muscle fibrillations, an early clinical sign in ALS.
source: This timing for delivery of the MuSK agonist antibody may be pertinent and significant for ALS, as denervation is the cause of muscle fibrillations, an early clinical sign in ALS.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about ALS clinical signs.

claim: At late stages of disease, a majority of synapses in SOD1-G93A mice are partially innervated.
source: However, ALS is a diagnosis of exclusion, leading to delays in diagnosis. Nonetheless, even at late stages of disease, a majority of synapses in SOD1-G93A mice are partially innervated, and the MuSK agonist antibody improved nerve terminal coverage at these partially innervated synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from the study.

claim: The loss of motor neurons during embryonic development is regulated, at least in part by synapse formation.
source: The loss of motor neurons during embryonic development is regulated, at least in part by synapse formation (Hollyday and Hamburger, 1976; Tanaka and Landmesser, 1986; Landmesser, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Adult motor neurons can receive trophic support from muscle.
source: The increased survival of motor neurons in MuSK agonist antibody-injected SOD1-G93A mice indicates that adult motor neurons can likewise receive trophic support from muscle.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of increased motor neuron survival in antibody-treated mice.

claim: The MuSK agonist antibody is effective at maintaining neuromuscular synapses in SOD1-G93A mice up to P162.
source: Although we used an agonist antibody to MuSK to stimulate retrograde signaling from muscle, one can envisage other approaches to stimulate MuSK or enhance retrograde signaling in order to maintain attachment of motor axons to muscle. The MuSK agonist antibody is effective at maintaining neuromuscular synapses in SOD1-G93A mice up to P162, but within the next week, synapses are lost, and the mice die.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing preserved synapses up to P162.

claim: The MuSK agonist antibody extended the lifespan of SOD1-G93A mice longer than riluzole, the long-standing FDA approved treatment for ALS.
source: Nonetheless, although the antibody cannot override the many pathological pathways that occur in the motor neuron and in non-neuronal cells, this therapeutic approach has a potent effect on the course of disease, reducing synaptic loss, improving motor output and extending the lifespan of SOD1-G93A mice longer than riluzole, the long-standing FDA approved treatment for ALS (Jablonski et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research comparing the effects of riluzole.

claim: Elimination of Bax, which prevents apoptotic cell death, fails to preserve neuromuscular synapses in SOD1-G93A mice.
source: Motor neuron cell death is a critical feature in ALS, but elimination of Bax, which prevents apoptotic cell death, fails to preserve neuromuscular synapses and increases survival of SOD1-G93A mice by only 20 days (Gould et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Elimination of Bax increases survival of SOD1-G93A mice by only 20 days.
source: Motor neuron cell death is a critical feature in ALS, but elimination of Bax, which prevents apoptotic cell death, fails to preserve neuromuscular synapses and increases survival of SOD1-G93A mice by only 20 days (Gould et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Neural Agrin and MuSK antibodies #13 and #22 stimulate MuSK tyrosine phosphorylation in C2 myotubes.
source: Neural Agrin and MuSK antibodies #13 and #22 stimulate MuSK tyrosine phosphorylation in C2 myotubes, whereas MuSK antibody #21 and a control antibody to Ragweed pollen (Rw) failed to stimulate MuSK phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: MuSK antibody #21 and a control antibody to Ragweed pollen failed to stimulate MuSK phosphorylation in C2 myotubes.
source: Neural Agrin and MuSK antibodies #13 and #22 stimulate MuSK tyrosine phosphorylation in C2 myotubes, whereas MuSK antibody #21 and a control antibody to Ragweed pollen (Rw) failed to stimulate MuSK phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The MuSK agonist antibody (Ab #13) failed to stimulate MuSK phosphorylation in innervated muscle.
source: The MuSK agonist antibody (Ab #13) failed to stimulate MuSK phosphorylation in innervated (Inn) muscle, suggesting that MuSK may be maximally phosphorylated at synapses by Agrin and Lrp4.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MuSK may be maximally phosphorylated at synapses by Agrin and Lrp4 in innervated muscle.
source: The MuSK agonist antibody (Ab #13) failed to stimulate MuSK phosphorylation in innervated (Inn) muscle, suggesting that MuSK may be maximally phosphorylated at synapses by Agrin and Lrp4.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the observation that Ab #13 failed to stimulate MuSK phosphorylation in innervated muscle.

claim: Ab #13 stimulated MuSK phosphorylation in denervated muscle by 2.2-fold.
source: Ab #13 stimulated MuSK phosphorylation in denervated muscle by 2.2-fold, demonstrating that Ab #13 activates MuSK in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ab #13 activates MuSK in vivo.
source: Ab #13 stimulated MuSK phosphorylation in denervated muscle by 2.2-fold, demonstrating that Ab #13 activates MuSK in vivo.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Ab #13 stimulated MuSK phosphorylation in denervated muscle.

claim: Following denervation, MuSK expression increases 7.5-fold.
source: Following denervation, MuSK expression increases 7.5-fold, but expression of Dok-7, an essential, inside-out activator of MuSK, increases only 2.0-fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Following denervation, expression of Dok-7 increases only 2.0-fold.
source: Following denervation, MuSK expression increases 7.5-fold, but expression of Dok-7, an essential, inside-out activator of MuSK, increases only 2.0-fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The activity of Ab #13 in denervated muscle may be limited by low non-synaptic Dok-7 expression.
source: Thus, the activity of Ab #13 in denervated muscle may be limited by low non-synaptic Dok-7 expression.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the observation that Dok-7 expression increases less than MuSK expression following denervation.

claim: Human and reverse chimera MuSK #13 antibodies are similarly effective in stimulating AChR clustering in C2C12 myotubes.
source: Human (h) and reverse chimera (rc) MuSK #13 antibodies are similarly effective in stimulating AChR clustering in C2C12 myotubes (n = 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Fab fragment from antibody #13 was unable to stimulate clustering of AChRs.
source: We found that the Fab fragment from antibody #13, unlike the intact IgG or the scFv, was unable to stimulate clustering of AChRs, indicating that antibodies must be dimeric and force-dimerize MuSK and promote an orientation that is favorable for trans-phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Antibodies must be dimeric and force-dimerize MuSK and promote an orientation that is favorable for trans-phosphorylation to stimulate AChR clustering.
source: We found that the Fab fragment from antibody #13, unlike the intact IgG or the scFv, was unable to stimulate clustering of AChRs, indicating that antibodies must be dimeric and force-dimerize MuSK and promote an orientation that is favorable for trans-phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Fab fragments failed to stimulate AChR clustering while intact IgG did.

claim: The reverse chimera MuSK antibody #13 has a half-life of 11 days following a single 10 mg/kg injection in wild type mice.
source: Following a single 10 mg/kg injection of reverse chimera MuSK agonist antibody #13 in wild type mice, the amount of antibody in the blood decreased over time as a single exponential with a half-life of 11 days.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Repeated 10 mg/kg injections of reverse chimera MuSK agonist antibody #13, every 24 days, in SOD1-G93A mice restored antibody levels and maintained the antibody at levels that were sufficient to saturate MuSK at the synapse.
source: Repeated 10 mg/kg injections of reverse chimera MuSK agonist antibody #13, every 24 days, in SOD1-G93A mice restored antibody levels and maintained the antibody at levels that were sufficient to saturate MuSK at the synapse.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The number of partially innervated synapses in SOD1-G93A mice is not altered by chronic injection of reverse chimera MuSK agonist antibody #13.
source: The number (~50%) of partially innervated synapses in SOD1-G93A mice is not altered by chronic injection of reverse chimera MuSK agonist antibody #13 ().
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The extent of the AChR-rich postsynaptic membrane that is apposed by nerve terminals is greater in SOD1-G93A mice injected with the MuSK agonist antibody than with a control antibody to GP120.
source: The extent of the AChR-rich postsynaptic membrane that is apposed by nerve terminals (NT) is greater in SOD1-G93A mice injected with the MuSK agonist antibody () than with a control antibody to GP120 ().
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: All mice included in this study had 21–26 copies of hSOD1-G93A.
source: All mice included in this study had 21–26 copies of hSOD1-G93A. The normalized hSOD1-G93A Ct values are shown for 25 samples (filled circles).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.
